topic: Sink-driven sugar flow through shared mycorrhizal hyphae: carbon is drawn to the strongest sink, which is the fungus, and heavy shade can reverse the flow into a recipient tree
summary: Mycorrhizal fungi act as the strongest sink for plant sugar. Carbon moves through shared hyphae toward carbon-limited trees, so flow follows source and sink conditions rather than a tree deliberately sharing. Heavy shade on a recipient tree can deplete its own roots of carbon. A 2016 labelled-CO2 study in spruce found label moving into neighbouring beech, pine and larch, in either direction. Experts still dispute how much of the flow is cooperation versus fungal demand, and how often networks are actually connected in the field.

facts.claim: Carbon flow from the donor tree is clear, given that the fungus is inherently heterotrophic and thus carbon-supply dependent.
facts.source_title: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy

facts.claim: Carbon flow through fungal mycelium is much more efficient than through bulk soil, supporting the idea that carbon moves through hyphal networks from one plant to another.
facts.source_title: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy

facts.claim: When a recipient tree is subjected to heavy shading, the roots of the recipient tree may experience carbon depletion.
facts.source_title: Belowground carbon transfer across mycorrhizal networks among trees: Facts, not fantasy

facts.claim: A 2016 study flooded the crowns of 120-year-old, 40-metre spruce trees with labelled carbon dioxide; the label appeared in neighbouring beech, pine or larch, and in the reverse direction, via shared fungal filaments.
facts.source_title: Trees Trade Carbon Among Each Other | News & Events | PSI

facts.claim: Researchers concluded that carbon is drawn to the strongest sink, namely mycorrhizal fungi, rather than being traded for nutrients.
facts.source_title: Are plants and fungi trading carbon for nutrients? Not likely, say researchers

facts.claim: The evidence for mycorrhizal networks facilitating tree cooperation is not as strong as the popular story would suggest.
facts.source_title: Do Trees Really Support Each Other through a Network of Fungi?

visualisable_mechanisms.name: fungal sink pull
visualisable_mechanisms.description: The hyphal network is a sugar sink. Carbon leaves a donor canopy tree and is drawn into the fungus, so flow depends on how much the fungus can absorb, not on a tree choosing to share.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Bright canopy nodes emit dots along thin branching hyphae into a central fungal web; the web thickens as it absorbs, and dot density follows its demand.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: shade reversal
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Heavy shade on a recipient tree cuts its own carbon supply, so the recipient's roots deplete and the net flow reverses toward it.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: One canopy node dims under a shadow band; its root tips fade while arrows along the hyphae flip direction, pulling sugar back toward the shaded tree.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: two-way species exchange
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Carbon moves across tree species in both directions through the same shared fungal filaments.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Spruce, beech, pine and larch nodes in four colours exchange paired dot streams along shared hyphae, with the direction of each stream changing over time.

visualisable_mechanisms.name: network thickening to steady state
visualisable_mechanisms.description: Connections form over time as hyphae grow between trees, then flows balance and the network settles into a steady pattern.
visualisable_mechanisms.render_or_sonify_hint: Over 20 seconds, sparse seedling-to-canopy threads branch and thicken, then the dot streams slow and reach an even, balanced rhythm.

open_questions: Does net carbon move between trees, or does the flow only reflect the fungus acting as a sink?
How often are mycorrhizal networks actually connected between trees in the field?
What share of transferred carbon ends up in recipient roots versus being used by the fungus?

surprise.justification: A generalist expects a mother tree sharing sugar with seedlings. What is true: carbon follows fungal sink demand and shade, and whether any cooperation exists is still disputed.
